parole.testo: From Latin Hadrianus (“from the Roman harbor Hadria”) a place name ultimately from Etruscan 𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀 (hatria). Doublet of Hadrian. See Adria.

parole.significato: An enclosed area, often outdoor, for the presentation of sporting events (sports arena) or other spectacular events; ea…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arēna (“sand; arena”), from earlier harēna, from Old Latin hasēna, possibly from Etruscan; compare Sabine fasēna.

parole.significato: A central room or space in ancient Roman homes, open to the sky in the middle; a similar space in other buildings.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrium (“entry hall”), from Etruscan.

parole.significato: A boy or younger man in a homoerotic relationship with an older man.
parole.testo: From Latin catamītus (“boy kept as a sexual partner”), from Catamītus, from Etruscan 𐌂𐌀𐌕𐌌𐌉𐌕𐌄 (catmite), from Ancient Greek Γανυμήδης (Ganumḗdēs, “Ganymede”), an attractive Trojan boy supposedly abducted to Mount Olympus by the god Zeus to become his cupbearer and lover. Doublet of Ganymede.

parole.significato: Any of several shrubs or trees of the genus Citrus in the family Rutaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin citrus (“a citron tree, thuja”), probably via Etruscan from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros); compare Middle English citurtre, cytyr tre. Thus a possible doublet of cedar.

parole.significato: An opening in a body, sometimes with a membrane.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fenestra. Existed in Middle English as fenestre, fenester, from Old English fenester (“window”).

From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄 (hercle), from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês), apparently cognate of Ἥρα (Hḗra, “Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (kléos, “glory”). Doublet of Heracles.

parole.significato: The household deities watching over one's family and tutelary deities watching over some public places.
parole.testo: From Latin Lares, plural form of lār, from Etruscan [Term?].

parole.significato: A minor addition to a text.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mantissa, mantīsa, of unknown origin (said by Festus to be a loanword from Etruscan, but it may actually be from Celtic, possibly through Etruscan mediation). Coincidentally, proparoxytone Greek μάντισσα (mántissa) means "female foreteller", as in χαρτομάντισσα (chartomántissa, “

parole.significato: That which is normal or typical.
parole.testo: From Latin norma (“a carpenter's square, a rule, a pattern, a precept”). Doublet of norma.

parole.significato: Sable (black), in the postmedieval practice of blazoning the tinctures in the arms of certain sovereign people and plac…
parole.testo: From Old English Sætern, from Latin Sāturnus, probably from Etruscan 𐌔𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌄 (satre), plausibly influenced by Latin satus, past participle of serere (“to sow”).

parole.significato: A posh young man from a privileged upper-class background.
parole.testo: From Latin Tarquinius from Etruscan tarqu(s)na, also tarcna or tarχna.

parole.significato: The name of a film, musical piece, painting, or other work of art.
parole.testo: From Middle English title, titel, from Old English titul (“title, heading, superscription”), from Latin titulus (“title, inscription”). Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, titlo, tittle, and titulus.
